spec: Count how many times a single decimal digit d (0-9) appears in the decimal representation of the absolute value of an integer n.
reference:
def count_digit_occurrences(n, d):
    return str(abs(n)).count(str(d))

spec: Convert a date given as (year, month, day) to its ordinal day count in the proleptic Gregorian calendar, where day 1 corresponds to January 1st of year 1. Assume the date is valid and year is a positive integer.

Write a function that, given a list of integers and an inclusive range [lo, hi], returns a sorted list of every integer in that range that does not appear in the list. Values in the list outside the range are ignored, and the list may be empty or contain duplicates.

Return True if the given string is a valid combined date and time in strict "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS" format (a valid ISO date, a single space, then a valid HH:MM:SS time with hours 0-23), and False otherwise.
Given a year and a month (1-12), return True if the 1st day of that month falls on a Saturday or Sunday, and False otherwise.

Join a list of strings into a natural-language list using commas, with 'and' before the last item. Zero items produce an empty string, one item is returned as-is, two items are joined as 'A and B', and three or more items are joined with commas and an oxford comma before 'and', like 'A, B, and C'.

Append the correct English ordinal suffix ('st', 'nd', 'rd', or 'th') to an integer, based on its last one or two digits: numbers ending in 11, 12, or 13 always use 'th'; otherwise numbers ending in 1, 2, or 3 use 'st', 'nd', 'rd' respectively, and all others use 'th'. Negative numbers use the suffix for their absolute value.
Group the non-empty strings in words by their first character. Return a dict mapping each first character to a sorted list of the words that start with it. An empty list returns an empty dict.

Scan through items from left to right, and after including each element, determine the most frequent element among those seen so far (ties broken by the smallest element). Return a list containing this running mode after each step, so the result has the same length as items.
Wrap a string in double quotes, escaping any internal double quote characters with a preceding backslash before wrapping.

Keep only the first maxlines lines of a multi-line text (lines separated by newlines) and, if there were more lines than that, append a final '...' line. If the text has maxlines lines or fewer, return it unchanged (joined by newlines).

Write a function that counts how many distinct sequences appear among all rotations of a list (moving some number of elements from the front to the back), treating rotations that produce the same sequence as one. An empty list counts as having exactly 1 (trivial) rotation.

Greedily word-wrap text so the first line may use the full width, while every following line is limited to width minus indent characters of words and then prefixed with that many spaces when returned (so its total printed length still fits in width). Return the list of resulting lines.
visible_tests: assert wrap_with_indent('one two three four five', 8, 2) == ['one two', '  three', '  four', '  five']
assert wrap_with_indent('a b c d e f', 3, 1) == ['a b', ' c', ' d', ' e', ' f']

spec: Write a function that shifts the elements of a list to the left by n positions, dropping the first n elements and filling the last n positions with a given fill value; the result has the same length as the input. If n is 0 or negative, return a copy of the list unchanged; if n is at least the length of the list, return a list of the fill value repeated to the original length.

Split text on whitespace into words and greedily pack them into lines of at most width characters, separated by single spaces, like a simple word wrap. Unlike a plain wrap, if a single word is longer than width, cut it into consecutive width-character chunks (each chunk its own line) until the remainder fits, then continue packing normally. Empty text returns an empty list.

Mask the local part of an email address (the part before the '@'): keep the first and last character visible and replace every character in between with '*', keeping the domain part unchanged. If the local part is only one character, leave it as-is; if it is two characters, mask the second with '*'.

Validate a credit-card-style string of the format 'XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX' where each X is a digit: exactly four groups of four digits separated by single spaces. Additionally the 16 digits (read without spaces) must pass the Luhn checksum (double every second digit from the right, subtracting 9 if over 9, and the total must be divisible by 10). Return True only if both the format and the checksum are valid.

Given a base slug string and a list of already-taken slug strings, return the base slug if it is not in the taken list; otherwise return the base slug suffixed with '-2', '-3', and so on, using the smallest suffix number starting at 2 that is not already taken.

Given a starting integer day number, a non-negative integer n, and a tuple of weekday numbers (0=Monday .. 6=Sunday) treated as non-business days, return the day number reached after moving forward n business days from the starting day (the starting day itself is not counted).
Convert a hyphen-separated slug string into a human-readable title by splitting on hyphens and capitalizing the first letter of each resulting word, joining them with single spaces.
reference:
def slug_to_title(s):
    return ' '.join(w.capitalize() for w in s.split('-'))

spec: Write a function that rotates a list by k positions where a positive k rotates left (front elements move to the back) and a negative k rotates right (back elements move to the front) by that many positions; k=0 leaves the list unchanged. k may have an absolute value larger than the list length. An empty list returns an empty list regardless of k.

Given a string s and an integer n, return s rotated right by n positions, meaning the last n characters are moved to the front of the string. n may be negative or larger than the length of s; the effective rotation should be computed modulo the length of s. An empty string always returns an empty string.

Write a function that returns the running (cumulative) product of a list of numbers as a new list of the same length, where each output element is the product of all input elements up to and including that position. An empty input produces an empty output.
reference:
def cumulative_product(lst):
    out = []
    p = 1
    for x in lst:
        p *= x
        out.append(p)
    return out

spec: Given an integer number of seconds elapsed since midnight (0 to 86399 inclusive), compute the number of seconds remaining until the next midnight.
reference:
def remaining_seconds_in_day(seconds_since_midnight):
    return 86400 - seconds_since_midnight

spec: Count how many integers in the inclusive range [a, b] (with a <= b) are evenly divisible by a positive integer k.
reference:
def count_multiples_in_range(a, b, k):
    return b // k - (a - 1) // k

spec: Validate a simple URL string. It must start with 'http://' or 'https://', contain no spaces anywhere, and be followed by a non-empty domain made of dot-separated labels (each label non-empty, alphanumeric with optional internal hyphens not at the start/end) with at least two labels and a purely alphabetic final label (TLD) of length at least 2. An optional path beginning with '/' may follow the domain with no further validation on the path other than containing no spaces.
Return a new string in which every character of the input string is duplicated (appears twice in a row), preserving the original order. An empty string returns an empty string.
reference:
def duplicate_each_char(s):
    return ''.join(ch * 2 for ch in s)

spec: Write a function that returns the sum of each contiguous window of length k from a list, in order, as a list of numbers. If k is not a positive integer at most the length of the list, return an empty list.

Given two dates date1 and date2 as (year, month, day) with date1 on or before date2, return the date that lies exactly halfway between them in days, rounding down (toward date1) when the number of days between them is odd.

Given a list of (time, priority, name) event tuples, return the names ordered by time ascending. If two events share the same time, order by priority ascending (a lower priority number means it is handled first). If both tie, order by name ascending. The input list may be empty.
reference:
def sort_events_by_time_then_priority(events):
    return [e[2] for e in sorted(events, key=lambda e: (e[0], e[1], e[2]))]

spec: Convert a date string of the form "D/M/YYYY" (day and month each one or two digits, year exactly four digits) into the zero-padded ISO form "YYYY-MM-DD".

Given a year, month, and an integer n (which may be negative), return the (year, month) tuple that results from adding n months to the given year and month, correctly rolling over across year boundaries. Day of month is not tracked.

Validate an IPv4 address string in dotted-quad notation. It must split by '.' into exactly 4 parts, each part consisting only of digits, representing a value from 0 to 255, and must not have a leading zero unless the part is exactly '0'. Return False if any rule is violated.

Validate an asterisk-masked card number string: it must be exactly 16 characters long, the first 12 characters must all be the asterisk character '*', and the last 4 characters must all be digits. Return False otherwise.

Given a valid clock hour (0-11) and minute (0-59), compute the absolute angle in degrees between the hour hand and the minute hand, returned as the smaller of the two possible angles (between 0 and 180 degrees inclusive).
Given a non-empty list of rows, where each row is a list of integers, compute the sum of each row, then return the median (as a float, using the odd/even averaging rule) of those row sums.

Compute the ordinal day of the year for a given date (year, month, day), where January 1st is day 1. The date is guaranteed valid, and leap years must be taken into account when the date falls after February.
Split a list of integers into two lists, preserving relative order: one containing the even numbers and one containing the odd numbers. Return them together as a tuple (evens, odds).
Given an even integer n >= 4, find a pair of prime numbers (p, q) with p <= q and p + q == n, choosing the smallest possible p. Return the pair as a tuple (p, q).
Convert a space-separated phrase into PascalCase by capitalizing each word and concatenating them with no separator.
reference:
def spaced_to_pascal(s):
    return ''.join(w.capitalize() for w in s.split())
